title: Two Brothers
full_review:
Some readers may recognize "Tiger, tiger burning bright" as a line from William Blake's poem "The Tiger." But for summer moviegoers it might also be the best way to summarize French director Jean-Jacques Annaud's captivating tiger tale, "Two Brothers" (Universal) -- a film burning bright with both beauty and heartfelt emotion.

In 1989, Annaud's "The Bear" struck a chord with audiences with its touching depiction of an orphaned grizzly cub left to fend for itself.

Annaud once again earns his stripes in "Two Brothers," combining stunning wildlife photography with sure-handed storytelling to craft a feel-good fable about the bonds of family and the healing power of love.

Set in the lush jungles of Southeast Asia, the film opens with two magnificent Bengal tigers frolicking like lovebirds among the exotic ruins of some ancient temple. They mate and give birth to a pair of cubs -- the pugnacious Kumal and his timid twin, Sangha.

As fate would have it, tragedy separates the two brothers soon after their birth. Kumal is sold off to a circus where, caged and abused, he comes to learn that the most savage of beasts is man. Inhumanely forced into submission by a sadistic tamer (Moussa Maaskri), Kumal is trained to growl on cue and jump through flaming hoops, declawed of his natural fighting spirit by depression and cruelty.

Initially, Sangha fares better. After being captured by a hunting party, he is adopted by the colonial governor's gentle-natured son, Raoul (Freddie Highmore), who lavishes affection on the jungle cat. But when a provoked Sangha mauls the family dog, he is shipped off, against Raoul's tear-filled protests, to the private menagerie of a local prince (Oanh Nyguen), where he is turned into a killer and made to fight for sport against other tigers.

Fully grown, the two brothers find themselves reunited in the arena during a royal festival. Pitted against each other as forced enemies, they must put their brotherly bonds to the ultimate test.

Guy Pearce plays a big-game hunter whose path becomes inextricably intertwined with those of the two tigers.

You don't have to be a fan of animal movies to recognize "Two Brothers" as a tour de force in family-friendly filmmaking. As a film, it is visually masterful, poetically poignant and extraordinarily entertaining.

Bold in his ambition to tell the story from the tigers' point of view, Annaud succeeds brilliantly in not only investing his striped stars with distinct personalities, but in making their complex inner life easy for human viewers to relate to on an emotional level. In fact, for a film where two tigers get the, er, lion's share of screen time, "Two Brothers" is suffused with remarkably rich humanity. And though this film contains considerably more dialogue than "The Bear," the most powerful moments are still those which unfold in silence.

Early on, the mother tigress cocks her head, alerted to the presence of the hunters, echoing in gesture the foreboding dread expressed by Bambi's mom's warning, "Man is in the forest" -- perhaps the most chilling line ever uttered on film. And while some sequences may be upsetting to very young children, most of the aforementioned mistreatment takes place off-screen.

The film definitely plays on viewers' emotions, but is done with such disarming grace that few but the most hardened cynics are likely to register complaint.

Though the story can be interpreted as conveying several messages, the simplest -- and, therefore, most profound -- is that love is stronger than hatred and cruelty.

Simply put, this marvelous and magical movie is -- to quote another famous tiger -- grrreat!

There is some minor violence and ongoing menace to the animals. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage.
